case.title: Reconcile and govern the Customer & Credit-Risk data model (FS data warehouse)
case.brief: You are joining as Data Analyst Manager and inheriting the `fs_dwh` analytics platform for a retail bank: a Snowflake-backed dbt project, a semantic/metrics layer, a partial data dictionary, and a Collibra-style governance export. Three teams — analytics, the regulatory reporting team, and a BI/self-serve group — already consume this model, and their definitions of core entities have drifted apart. Leadership wants 'one governed source of truth' for the Customer and Credit-Risk domain, but the request arrived through a recruiter-aggregator template and the actual modeling/governance standard is not written down anywhere. Your job is to act as the steward: decide the canonical definitions, encode them in the model and semantic layer, set the minimum documentation/metadata standard, and make sure you do not silently change numbers that regulatory or risk consumers depend on. The provided materials fit this role directly — work on them. Treat this as ~2 hours of real stewardship work: depth and defensible judgment matter far more than touching every file. The code itself can be generated; what we are reading is the path you take through the ambiguity, so keep a running DECISIONS log as normal practice. Do not invent data volumes or business rules you cannot ground in the provided files — where the materials are silent, that is a decision to record, not a fact to fabricate.
case.repoSeed:
A representative (synthetic) financial-services analytics workspace, `fs_dwh/`:

- `models/staging/stg_core_banking__accounts.sql`, `stg_core_banking__transactions.sql` — staging over core-banking feeds. The transactions stream carries `transaction_type` ∈ {POSTING, REVERSAL, ADJUSTMENT} and a nullable `reversal_of_txn_id`; reversals and adjustments are appended as new positive-amount rows rather than negative offsets.
- `models/marts/dim_customer.sql` — current customer dimension; derives an `is_active` flag as 'transacted in the last 90 days'.
- `models/marts/fct_transactions.sql` — fact table that naively unions all transaction rows; amounts are stored as unsigned magnitudes.
- `models/marts/mart_risk_exposure.sql` — the risk mart that finance and regulatory reporting read; it computes exposure and a `default_flag` using `days_past_due > 60`, and — critically — still LEFT JOINs the legacy `legacy/vw_customer_segments.sql` for its segment column.
- `legacy/vw_customer_segments.sql` — a hand-maintained SQL view with hardcoded segment thresholds, predating dbt; `dim_customer` was supposed to replace it but never fully did.
- `models/semantic/metrics.yml` — semantic-layer metrics (`active_customers`, `default_rate`, `net_exposure`); `active_customers` here is defined as 'customer has ≥1 open account', which disagrees with `dim_customer.is_active`.
- `models/marts/schema.yml` — sparse dbt docs and a couple of `unique`/`not_null` tests.
- `reports/regulatory/credit_risk_report_spec.md` — the regulatory spec: default is '≥90 days past due' (IFRS 9 framing) and an 'active relationship' for AML/KYC purposes means 'any account with activity in the last 12 months'.
- `data_dictionary.csv` — ~30 columns, inconsistently filled: some have descriptions, almost none have an owner/steward, PII classification, or regulatory/lineage tags.
- `governance/collibra_export.json` — stewardship and lineage records with obvious gaps (orphaned terms, no steward on key assets).
- `README.md` — thin; says 'standardize the data dictionary and unify customer/risk definitions' without defining the target standard or naming the consumers.
tasks: Reconcile the canonical definitions for the Customer & Credit-Risk domain. 'Active customer' is currently defined three ways (dim_customer.is_active = 90-day behavioral; metrics.yml = has-open-account; the regulatory spec = 12-month AML activity), and 'default/delinquency' is 60 DPD in mart_risk_exposure but 90 DPD in credit_risk_report_spec.md. Choose ONE canonical definition for each (or a small set of explicitly-scoped, named variants), encode them consistently across dim_customer.sql, metrics.yml, and mart_risk_exposure.sql, and write the governed definition into data_dictionary.csv. State which consumer each definition serves.

Make the model trustworthy before it is 'unified': handle the legacy `legacy/vw_customer_segments.sql` dependency in mart_risk_exposure.sql without silently shifting the exposure and default numbers that regulatory/finance consumers rely on, and reconcile the transaction grain in fct_transactions.sql so that exposure totals are correct given REVERSAL/ADJUSTMENT rows. Show a before/after check (counts AND a financial total, not just 'it compiles') that demonstrates whether any consumer-visible number moved, and say why that movement is or is not acceptable.

Set the minimum governed metadata standard for this domain and apply it. Decide which attributes are mandatory for a column to be 'documented' here (e.g. description, owning steward, PII classification, regulatory/lineage tag — you choose the bar and justify it for an FS context), then apply that standard to the Customer + Transaction columns in data_dictionary.csv and align the relevant entries in governance/collibra_export.json. Do not boil the ocean — cover the domain at the depth the timebox allows and note what you deliberately deferred.

Keep a short DECISIONS.md as you go (this is normal stewardship practice, not a separate write-up): for every call where the brief/README was open — canonical definitions, legacy handling, transaction grain, the metadata bar — record what you chose, the alternative you rejected and why, and the one question you would have put to the analytics / regulatory / BI stakeholders before committing.

coverProbes.where: Conflict across dim_customer.is_active (90-day behavioral), metrics.yml active_customers (has-open-account), and credit_risk_report_spec.md (12-month AML activity).
coverProbes.reveals: A naive candidate picks whichever definition is easiest to code, or 'unifies' all three into one number, flattening a real semantic distinction and likely breaking a regulatory metric. A strong candidate recognizes these serve different consumers, names who owns each, and either selects one canonical default with clearly-scoped named variants or escalates the choice — and crucially understands that 'active' for marketing analytics is not 'active' for AML.
decisionSpace: Pick behavioral 90-day as the canonical default (serves analytics/engagement), and expose the others as explicitly-named variant metrics — optimizes for the largest consumer, risks regulatory teams quietly diverging again.

Make the regulatory/AML 12-month definition canonical because it is the externally-governed one, and re-label the behavioral metric as 'recently_active' — safest for compliance, but may surprise BI users whose dashboards shift.

Refuse a single canonical 'active' and instead govern three named, separately-owned metrics with shared lineage — most honest to reality, but pushes the disambiguation cost onto every consumer and the catalog.

coverProbes.where: mart_risk_exposure.sql still LEFT JOINs legacy/vw_customer_segments.sql for segment, even though dim_customer was meant to replace it.
coverProbes.reveals: A candidate who regenerates dim_customer or 'cleans up' the join without reading the downstream mart either breaks segment population or silently changes risk numbers. A strong candidate traces the dependency first, recognizes the legacy view is load-bearing for a regulated consumer, and chooses a migration path that protects the numbers rather than assuming the new model is a drop-in replacement.
decisionSpace: Cut over fully to dim_customer and delete the legacy view — cleanest end state, but requires proving segment parity and risks moving regulatory figures now.
Keep the legacy view behind a compatibility shim / aliased model and deprecate with a dated plan — protects current numbers, but prolongs the duplicate definition.
Leave the join untouched, document the discrepancy and lineage, and scope the migration as separate governed work — lowest risk this session, but defers the actual unification the brief asked for.

coverProbes.where: fct_transactions.sql unions REVERSAL/ADJUSTMENT rows as additional positive-amount records; exposure and default_rate sum unsigned magnitudes.
coverProbes.reveals: Naive one-shot generation produces a SUM(amount) that passes the existing unique/not_null and row-count tests and 'looks plausible', but double-counts reversed and adjusted transactions — materially overstating exposure, exactly the kind of error a regulator catches. A strong candidate verifies against a known financial total or reconstructs net movement, detects the inflation, and fixes the grain rather than trusting the row-level check.
decisionSpace: Exclude REVERSAL/ADJUSTMENT rows from exposure measures and document them as non-economic events — simple and correct for totals, but loses auditability of why a figure changed.
Net transactions by signing amounts via reversal_of_txn_id so the fact stays at event grain but measures net out — preserves audit trail, more complex and must handle partial/chained reversals.
Keep gross rows but introduce an explicit `net_amount` / settled-only measure used by the risk mart, leaving gross for ops — most flexible, but adds a metric the catalog and consumers must learn.

coverProbes.where: README asks to 'standardize the data dictionary' with no target standard; data_dictionary.csv and collibra_export.json have descriptions but mostly no steward, PII class, or regulatory/lineage tag.
coverProbes.reveals: A naive candidate fills in free-text descriptions and calls the dictionary 'standardized', missing that in FS the governed value is ownership, PII handling, and regulatory lineage. A strong candidate defines an explicit, defensible minimum bar appropriate to a regulated domain, applies it consistently to a bounded scope, and states what was deferred rather than pretending full coverage.
decisionSpace: Lightweight bar — mandatory description + owning steward only — fast to reach across all columns, but leaves PII/regulatory exposure ungoverned.

Compliance-first bar — steward + PII classification + regulatory/lineage tag mandatory, descriptions best-effort — strongest for an FS audit, but slower so only part of the domain gets fully tagged in the timebox.
Tiered bar — strict mandatory set for risk/PII-bearing columns, lighter set for the rest — pragmatic and risk-weighted, but requires defining and defending the tiering rule itself.
